en: Saṁyutta Nikāya 40.1 (SN 40.1, PTS SN iv 262) 1. Moggallāna-vagga Paṭhama-jhāna-pañhā-sutta The First Discourse on Questions Concerning Jhāna At Sāvatthī. There, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this: “Friends, how many things does one who is not skilled in jhāna need to develop? “Friend, one who is not skilled in jhāna needs to develop five things. “And what, friend, are those five things that one who is not skilled in jhāna needs to develop? Here, friend, a bhikkhu develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. He develops right view, which is based upon seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release. These, friend, are the five things that one who is not skilled in jhāna needs to develop. “But, friend, how many things does one who is skilled in jhāna need to develop? “Friend, one who is skilled in jhāna needs to develop two things. “And what, friend, are those two things that one who is skilled in jhāna needs to develop? Here, friend, a bhikkhu develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. These, friend, are the two things that one who is skilled in jhāna needs to develop. “But, friend, how many things does one who is skilled in jhāna need to abandon? “Friend, one who is skilled in jhāna needs to abandon two things. “And what, friend, are those two things that one who is skilled in jhāna needs to abandon? Here, friend, a bhikkhu abandons ill will and malevolence; he abandons anger and resentment. These, friend, are the two things that one who is skilled in jhāna needs to abandon. “But, friend, how many things does one who is skilled in jhāna need to cultivate? “Friend, one who is skilled in jhāna needs to cultivate two things. “And what, friend, are those two things that one who is skilled in jhāna needs to cultivate? Here, friend, a bhikkhu cultivates loving-kindness toward his own teacher; he cultivates compassion toward his fellow monks. These, friend, are the two things that one who is skilled in jhāna needs to cultivate. “But, friend, how many things does one who is skilled in jhāna need to protect? “Friend, one who is skilled in jhāna needs to protect one thing. “And what, friend, is that one thing that one who is skilled in jhāna needs to protect? Here, friend, a bhikkhu protects the mind with mindfulness. This, friend, is the one thing that one who is skilled in jhāna needs to protect. “But, friend, how many things does one who is skilled in jhāna need to penetrate? “Friend, one who is skilled in jhāna needs to penetrate one thing.

“And what, friend, is that one thing that one who is skilled in jhāna needs to penetrate? Here, friend, a bhikkhu penetrates the mind with wisdom. This, friend, is the one thing that one who is skilled in jhāna needs to penetrate. “But, friend, how many things does one who is skilled in jhāna need to fulfill? “Friend, one who is skilled in jhāna needs to fulfill one thing. “And what, friend, is that one thing that one who is skilled in jhāna needs to fulfill? Here, friend, a bhikkhu fulfills the Noble Eightfold Path. This, friend, is the one thing that one who is skilled in jhāna needs to fulfill. “But, friend, how many things does one who is skilled in jhāna need to understand? “Friend, one who is skilled in jhāna needs to understand one thing. “And what, friend, is that one thing that one who is skilled in jhāna needs to understand? Here, friend, a bhikkhu understands the mind as it really is. This, friend, is the one thing that one who is skilled in jhāna needs to understand. “But, friend, how many things does one who is skilled in jhāna need to realize? “Friend, one who is skilled in jhāna needs to realize one thing. “And what, friend, is that one thing that one who is skilled in jhāna needs to realize? Here, friend, a bhikkhu realizes Nibbāna, the unconditioned. This, friend, is the one thing that one who is skilled in jhāna needs to realize. When this was said, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna rose from his seat and departed. Not long after the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna had left, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported everything that had occurred, exactly as it had been said. “Good, good, Ānanda! Moggallāna is wise, Ānanda; Moggallāna has great discernment, Ānanda. If, Ānanda, you were to ask me about these very things, I would answer you in exactly the same way as Moggallāna has answered you. It is because I have taught the Dhamma by way of such analysis, Ānanda, that when Moggallāna was asked these questions, he was able to answer them just as he did. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, the bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. (This concludes the first discourse on questions concerning jhāna in the Moggallāna-vagga.)
On one occasion the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the bhikkhus:
“Friends, bhikkhus!”
“Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this:
“In this case, friends, while I was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in my mind thus:”
‘The first jhāna, the first jhāna,’ it is said.
What now is the first jhāna?
Then, friends, this occurred to me:

‘Here, bhikkhus, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
This is called the first jhāna.

Friends, I too, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
"Friends, while I was dwelling in this state of abiding, perceptions and mental applications associated with sensual desire arose within me.
Then, friends, the Blessed One approached me by means of his psychic power and said:
'Moggallāna, Moggallāna!'"
“Do not be negligent, brahmin; settle the mind in the first jhāna, unify the mind in the first jhāna, concentrate the mind in the first jhāna.

Then, friends, at a later time, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
For if one were speaking rightly, friends, it would be said of me: [that I am so].
“If one were to speak rightly of anyone, saying: ‘Supported by the Teacher, this disciple has attained great direct knowledge,’ it is of me that one would rightly say:
‘Supported by the Teacher, this disciple has attained great direct knowledge.
This was the first.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 40.2 (SN 40.2, PTS SN iv 263) 1. Moggallāna-vagga The Discourse on the Question Concerning the Second Jhāna At Sāvatthī. There, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this: “Friends, when a bhikkhu possesses four qualities, it is fitting for him to enter and dwell in the second jhāna. What four? Here, friends, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest transgressions; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This, friends, is the first quality that a bhikkhu must possess so that it is fitting for him to enter and dwell in the second jhāna. Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has heard much, has retained what he has heard, has stored up what he has heard. Whatever teachings are admirable in the beginning, admirable in the middle, and admirable in the end, which proclaim the holy life in its spirit and in its letter, entirely complete, perfectly pure, and purified: such teachings he has heard much of, retained, recited verbally, mentally examined, and penetrated well through view. This, friends, is the second quality that a bhikkhu must possess so that it is fitting for him to enter and dwell in the second jhāna. Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. This, friends, is the third quality that a bhikkhu must possess so that it is fitting for him to enter and dwell in the second jhāna. Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is one who understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, friends, is the fourth quality that a bhikkhu must possess so that it is fitting for him to enter and dwell in the second jhāna. When a bhikkhu possesses these four qualities, it is fitting for him to enter and dwell in the second jhāna. [The Buddha then said: “It is wonderful, Moggallāna! It is amazing, Moggallāna! How well this has been spoken by you, Moggallāna! But, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu who possesses five qualities is fit to enter and dwell in the second jhāna. What five? Here, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu is virtuous... [as before] ...he trains in them. This, Moggallāna, is the first quality... Furthermore, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu has heard much... [as before] ...penetrated well through view. This, Moggallāna, is the second quality... Furthermore, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. This, Moggallāna, is the third quality... Furthermore, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu is one who understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... [as before] ...‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, Moggallāna, is the fourth quality... Furthermore, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu is one who understands as it really is: ‘This is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. This, Moggallāna, is the fifth quality that a bhikkhu must possess so that it is fitting for him to enter and dwell in the second jhāna. When a bhikkhu possesses these five qualities, it is fitting for him to enter and dwell in the second jhāna. Thus spoke the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Having said this, the Teacher further said this: “When a bhikkhu is virtuous, learned, Gained the jhānas and knows the Dhamma, He understands suffering as it is, Its origin, its cessation, and the path. Such a one, having known the Dhamma, Is fit to enter the second jhāna.”
“‘The second jhāna, the second jhāna,’ it is said.
What now is the second jhāna?
Then, friends, this occurred to me:”

‘Here, friend, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and singleness of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
This is called the second jhāna.

Thus, friend, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and singleness of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
"Friend, as I was dwelling in this abiding, perceptions and mental engagements accompanied by applied thought occurred to me.
Then, friend, the Blessed One approached me by means of his psychic power and said:
'Moggallāna, Moggallāna!'"
“Do not be negligent regarding the second jhāna, brahmin; steady the mind in the second jhāna, unify the mind in the second jhāna, concentrate the mind in the second jhāna.

Then, friends, after some time, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and unification of mind, is without applied thought and without sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
For if one were speaking rightly, friends, one would say of that:
“If one were to speak rightly of anyone, it would be of me when saying:
‘Supported by the Teacher, this disciple has attained great direct knowledge. This is the second [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 40.3 (SN 40.3, PTS SN iv 264) 1. Moggallāna-vagga The Discourse on the Question Concerning the Third Jhāna “Venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the arising of the third jhāna? “The third jhāna, Ānanda, arises with the second jhāna as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the arising of the second jhāna? “The second jhāna, Ānanda, arises with the first jhāna as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the arising of the first jhāna? “The first jhāna, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of the body as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of the body? “The seclusion of the body, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of speech as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of speech? “The seclusion of speech, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of the mind as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of the mind? “The seclusion of the mind, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of views as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of views? “The seclusion of views, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of doubt as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of doubt? “The seclusion of doubt, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of virtue as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of virtue? “The seclusion of virtue, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of wealth as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of wealth? “The seclusion of wealth, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of birth as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of birth? “The seclusion of birth, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of name-and-form as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of name-and-form? “The seclusion of name-and-form, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of consciousness as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of consciousness? “The seclusion of consciousness, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of formations as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of formations? “The seclusion of formations, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of ignorance as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of ignorance? “The seclusion of ignorance, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of craving as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of craving? “The seclusion of craving, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of feeling as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of feeling? “The seclusion of feeling, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of contact as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of contact? “The seclusion of contact, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of the six sense bases as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of the six sense bases? “The seclusion of the six sense bases, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of name-and-form as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of name-and-form? “The seclusion of name-and-form, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of consciousness as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of consciousness? “The seclusion of consciousness, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of formations as its cause and condition. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for the seclusion of formations? “The seclusion of formations, Ānanda, arises with the seclusion of ignorance as its cause and condition. “Thus, Ānanda, with the seclusion of ignorance as condition, there is the seclusion of formations; with the seclusion of formations as condition, there is the seclusion of consciousness; with the seclusion of consciousness as condition, there is the seclusion of name-and-form; with the seclusion of name-and-form as condition, there is the seclusion of the six sense bases; with the seclusion of the six sense bases as condition, there is the seclusion of contact; with the seclusion of contact as condition, there is the seclusion of feeling; with the seclusion of feeling as condition, there is the seclusion of craving; with the seclusion of craving as condition, there is the seclusion of ignorance.”
“‘The third jhāna, the third jhāna,’ it is said.
What now is the third jhāna?
Then, friends, this occurred to me:”
Here, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells equanimous and mindful, clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body;
he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous."
This is called the third jhāna.
"Friends, with the fading away of rapture, I dwelt equanimous and mindful, clearly comprehending, and experienced happiness with the body;
of which the Noble Ones declare: ‘He dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous.’"
I entered and dwelt in the third jhāna.
While I was dwelling in this state of abiding, friends, perceptions and mental applications accompanied by rapture occurred to me.
Then, friends, the Blessed One approached me by means of his psychic power and said this:
“‘Moggallāna, Moggallāna!
Do not be negligent regarding the third jhāna, brahmin; settle the mind in the third jhāna, unify the mind in the third jhāna, and concentrate the mind in the third jhāna.
Then, friends, at a later time, with the fading away of rapture, I dwelt equanimous and mindful.”
“Mindful, I experienced pleasure with the body; that which the Noble Ones describe as ‘dwelling in happiness, mindful and equanimous’—thus I entered and dwelt in the third jhāna.
For, friends, one who speaks rightly could say of me: ‘He has attained great direct knowledge.’”
The Third.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 40.4 (SN 40.4, PTS SN iv 265) 1.
Moggallāna Vagga
The Discourse on the Question Concerning the Fourth Jhāna:
“‘The fourth jhāna, the fourth jhāna,’ it is said.
What now is the fourth jhāna?”
Then, friends, it occurred to me:

“Here, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
This is called the fourth jhāna.”

"Thus, friends, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I entered and dwelt in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
While I was dwelling in this state, friends, perceptions and mental engagements accompanied by pleasure occurred to me.
Then, friends, the Blessed One approached me by means of his psychic power and said this:"
“‘Moggallāna, Moggallāna!
Do not be negligent regarding the fourth jhāna, brahmin; settle the mind in the fourth jhāna, unify the mind in the fourth jhāna, and concentrate the mind in the fourth jhāna.
Then, friends, at a later time, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, even before...”
With the subsiding of both joy and grief, I entered and dwelt in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
For, friend, one who would speak rightly of it... [as before] ...has attained great direct knowledge.”
The Fourth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 40.5 (SN 40.5, PTS SN iv 266) 1.
Moggallāna Chapter
The Discourse on the Question Concerning the Base of Infinite Space:
“‘The base of infinite space, the base of infinite space,’ it is said.
What now is the base of infinite space?”
Then, friends, this occurred to me:

“Here, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
This is called the base of infinite space.”

"Thus, friends, with the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory reaction, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking 'space is infinite,' I entered and dwelt in the base of infinite space.
While I was dwelling in this state, friends, perceptions and mental engagements associated with form occurred to me.
Then, friends, the Blessed One approached me by means of his psychic power and said this:"
“‘Moggallāna, Moggallāna!

Do not be negligent regarding the base of infinite space, brahmin; settle the mind in the base of infinite space, unify the mind in the base of infinite space, and concentrate the mind in the base of infinite space.

Then, friends, after some time, with the complete transcending of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ I entered and dwelt in the base of infinite space.”
"For if one were speaking rightly, friend, it would be of him... he has attained great direct knowledge.
The fifth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 40.6 (SN 40.6, PTS SN iv 266)
1. Moggallāna Chapter:
The Discourse on the Question Concerning the Base of Infinite Consciousness “It is said, ‘the base of infinite consciousness, the base of infinite consciousness.’”
"What, then, is the base of infinite consciousness?
Friends, this occurred to me:
"In this case, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking 'consciousness is infinite,' enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness."
‘This is called the base of infinite consciousness.
Then, friends, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, perceiving ‘consciousness is infinite,’ I entered and dwelt in the base of infinite consciousness.
While I was dwelling in this state, friends, perceptions and mental engagements associated with the base of infinite space still occurred to me.
Then, friends, the Blessed One approached me by means of his psychic power and said this:
“Moggallāna, Moggallāna!

Do not be negligent regarding the base of infinite consciousness, brahmin; settle the mind upon the base of infinite consciousness, unify the mind upon the base of infinite consciousness, and concentrate the mind upon the base of infinite consciousness.”
"Then, friends, on a later occasion, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, perceiving 'consciousness is infinite,' I entered and dwelt in the base of infinite consciousness.
For if one were speaking rightly, friends, one would say of me: ... [omitted] ... 'He has attained great direct knowledge.
(The sixth.)

Saṃyutta Nikāya 40.7 (SN 40.7, PTS SN iv 267) 1. Moggallāna-vagga The Discourse on the Question Concerning the Base of Nothingness (Ākiñcaññāyatana-pañha-sutta) At Sāvatthī. “Moggallāna, when a bhikkhu is liberated in mind through the base of nothingness, he is said to have attained the fruit of the non-returner. “Venerable sir, how does a bhikkhu become one who has attained the fruit of the non-returner by being liberated in mind through the base of nothingness? “Here, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. He attends to that attainment with mindfulness. As he attends to it with mindfulness, his mind becomes liberated from the taints. Thus, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu is liberated in mind through the base of nothingness and is said to have attained the fruit of the non-returner. “Venerable sir, how does a bhikkhu become one who has attained final knowledge by being liberated in mind through the base of nothingness? “Here, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He attends to that attainment with mindfulness. As he attends to it with mindfulness, his mind becomes liberated from the taints. Thus, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu is liberated in mind through the base of nothingness and is said to have attained final knowledge. “Venerable sir, how does a bhikkhu become one who has attained final knowledge by being liberated in mind through the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception? “Here, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu, having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. Having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed. Thus, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu is liberated in mind through the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and is said to have attained final knowledge. [The Buddha then repeated the entire sequence of attainments, from the base of infinite space up to the cessation of perception and feeling, for each of the three types of disciples: those who have attained the fruit of the non-returner, those who have attained final knowledge, and those whose taints are utterly destroyed. “Venerable sir, how does a bhikkhu become one who has attained the fruit of the non-returner by being liberated in mind through the base of infinite space? “Here, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. He attends to that attainment with mindfulness. As he attends to it with mindfulness, his mind becomes liberated from the taints. Thus, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu is liberated in mind through the base of infinite space and is said to have attained the fruit of the non-returner. [The Buddha then repeated the entire sequence of attainments, from the base of infinite space up to the cessation of perception and feeling, for each of the three types of disciples. “Venerable sir, how does a bhikkhu become one who has attained final knowledge by being liberated in mind through the base of infinite space? “Here, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. He attends to that attainment with mindfulness. As he attends to it with mindfulness, his mind becomes liberated from the taints. Thus, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu is liberated in mind through the base of infinite space and is said to have attained final knowledge. [The Buddha then repeated the entire sequence of attainments, from the base of infinite space up to the cessation of perception and feeling, for each of the three types of disciples. “Venerable sir, how does a bhikkhu become one who has attained final knowledge by being liberated in mind through the base of nothingness? [The Buddha then repeated the entire sequence of attainments, from the base of nothingness up to the cessation of perception and feeling, for each of the three types of disciples. “Venerable sir, how does a bhikkhu become one who has attained final knowledge by being liberated in mind through the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception? [The Buddha then repeated the entire sequence of attainments, from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception up to the cessation of perception and feeling, for each of the three types of disciples. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, the venerable Mahāmoggallāna delighted in the words of the Blessed One. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, the venerable Mahāmoggallāna delighted in the words of the Blessed One. This is the first discourse in this section. The section on Moggallāna is concluded. The fourth book is finished. The Saṃyutta Nikāya is finished. The collection of discourses is finished. The basket of the Dhamma is finished. The dispensation of the Teacher is finished. May there be peace. May there be well-being. May there be prosperity. May there be happiness. May all beings be happy. May all beings be well. May all beings be prosperous. May all beings be happy. May all beings be well. May all beings be prosperous. May all beings be happy. May all beings be well. May all beings be prosperous. May all beings be happy. May all beings be well. May all beings be prosperous. May all beings be happy. May all beings be well. May all beings be prosperous. May all beings be happy. May all beings be well. May all beings be prosperous. May all beings be happy. May all beings be well. May all beings be prosperous. May all beings be happy. May all beings be well. May all beings be prosperous. May all beings be happy. "'The base of nothingness, the base of nothingness,' it is said.
What now is the base of nothingness?
Then, friends, this occurred to me:
‘Here, bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, [perceiving] “there is nothing,” one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
This is called the base of nothingness.
So, friend, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving “there is nothing,” I enter and dwell in the base of nothingness.
"Friends, as I was dwelling in this abiding, perceptions and mental engagements associated with the base of infinite consciousness arose within me.
Then, friends, the Blessed One approached me by means of his psychic power and said:
'Moggallāna, Moggallāna!'"

“Do not be negligent regarding the base of nothingness, brahmin; steady your mind upon the base of nothingness, unify your mind upon the base of nothingness, and concentrate your mind upon the base of nothingness.
Then, friends, after some time, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking “there is nothing,” I entered and dwelt in the base of nothingness.
Friends, if one were speaking rightly, it would be said of me: “… he has attained great direct knowledge.”

The Discourse on the Question Concerning the Base of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception: “‘The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,’ it is said.
What, then, is the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?”
Then, friends, it occurred to me:
“Here, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is called the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”
"Then, friends, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, I entered and dwelt in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
While I was dwelling in this state, friends, perceptions and mental engagements associated with the base of nothingness still occurred to me.
Then the Blessed One, having approached me through his psychic power, said this:"
“‘Moggallāna, Moggallāna!

Do not be negligent regarding the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, brahmin; settle the mind in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, unify the mind in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and concentrate the mind in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Then, friends, at a later time, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, I entered and dwelt in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”
"For if one were speaking rightly, friend, one would say of him: ... [as before] ... he has attained great direct knowledge.

1. Moggallāna Chapter:
The Discourse on the Question Concerning the Signless “It is said, ‘the signless concentration of mind, the signless concentration of mind.’”
"What, then, is the signless concentration of mind?
Then, friends, this occurred to me:
"Here, a bhikkhu, through non-attention to all signs, enters and dwells in the signless concentration of mind."
‘This is called the signless concentration of mind.
Thus, friends, by not attending to any signs, I entered and dwelt in the signless concentration of mind.
While I was dwelling in this state, friends, my consciousness followed after signs.
Then, friends, the Blessed One approached me by means of his psychic power and said this:
“Moggallāna, Moggallāna!

Do not be negligent, brahmin, regarding the signless concentration of mind; steady your mind in the signless concentration of mind, unify your mind in the signless concentration of mind, and compose your mind in the signless concentration of mind.”
Then, friends, on a later occasion, through non-attention to all signs, I entered and dwelt in the signless concentration of mind.
Friends, if one speaking rightly were to say of anyone:
"A disciple who has been favored by the Teacher has attained great direct knowledge," it is of me that one would rightly say this.
“A disciple, supported by the Teacher, has attained great direct knowledge.
Thus [he spoke].

The tenth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 40.11 (SN 40.11, PTS SN iv 280) 1. Moggallānavagga Candanasutta “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a man who, having taken sandalwood from the Himalayas, would burn it in a fire. As he burned it, he would sprinkle it with water from the Ganges. What do you think, bhikkhus? Would that man be able to extinguish that fire by sprinkling it with water from the Ganges? “No, venerable sir. “That man would not be able to extinguish that fire by sprinkling it with water from the Ganges. Why is that? Because that fire would be great and powerful, while the water from the Ganges would be little. So too, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has abandoned the five lower fetters, it is impossible that he will not attain final nibbāna right here. Why is that? Because his destination is fixed, his future existence is certain.”
